title: How the US Interstate System Works
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of the US Interstate Highway System, from early dirt-road conditions and the good roads movement, through the Lincoln Highway, the American Association of State Highway Officials, and the Pershing/McDonald map, to Eisenhower's Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956 and its Cold War and economic motivations. They cover the funding debate over toll roads versus gas and tire taxes, the Chicago test tracks, highway revolts such as Jane Jacobs' fight against the Manhattan expressway, interstate design standards and safety statistics, numbering and concurrency quirks, and the mixed social and economic effects. The episode also includes a sponsor break, a few tangents about rock musicians and Montana speed laws, and a listener mail segment about punk and hardcore.
topics: American Association of State Highway Officials

segments.title: Cold open and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug upcoming live shows in Orlando and New Orleans, joke about Aretha Franklin and Led Zeppelin, and introduce the episode topic of the US interstate system.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live shows

segments.title: Overview of the interstate network
segments.summary: The hosts describe the interstate system as roughly 48,000 miles of limited-access highway connecting major US cities, and compare it to a circulatory or nervous system.

segments.title: Early 20th-century dirt roads and the good roads movement
segments.summary: Rural roads in the early 1900s were mostly dirt and muddy, and bicycle enthusiasts and wealthy car owners launched the good roads movement. Rural free delivery mail legislation added pressure for better roads.

segments.title: Lincoln Highway and early private road groups
segments.summary: The Lincoln Highway was the first transcontinental highway, built largely by connecting and improving existing roads. Carl G. Fisher, an Indiana entrepreneur and racing enthusiast, promoted it. Private auto clubs initially shaped roads.

segments.title: American Association of State Highway Officials and numbering
segments.summary: The AASHO, a non-government group formed around 1914, set highway best practices and influenced which roads became highways. Federal Aid Road Act funding followed, and highways were numbered, with US 50 explained as the reason there is no I-50.
topics: American Association of State Highway Officials

segments.title: Transition to the interstate idea
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish older US highways from the later interstates and explain that growing car use made highway improvement a rising priority, which led to the interstate concept.

segments.title: FDR's 1938 plan, post-war economics, and the Pershing/McDonald map
segments.summary: Roosevelt proposed a system of superhighways, delayed by World War II. Post-war boom concerns and public works job creation are discussed. Thomas McDonald's map, handed to Congress by General Pershing in the 1920s, became the blueprint for the interstate system.

segments.title: Eisenhower, Cold War defense, and reasons for the interstates
segments.summary: Eisenhower pushed the 1956 Federal Aid Highway Act, with military and Cold War evacuation rationales, the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways name, urban-to-rural commuting, leisure travel, and safety. Economic benefits of connecting rural areas to cities are discussed.
topics: National System of Interstate and Defense Highways

segments.title: Interstate safety design and toll road debate
segments.summary: Interstates are safer than highways due to divided lanes, controlled access, overpasses, and ramps. Eisenhower originally wanted toll roads, but studies showed tolls rarely pay for themselves; Georgia 400 is an example. Trucking and tire interests shaped the gas and tire tax, and the National Highway Users Conference promoted the freeway concept.

segments.title: Highway Trust Fund, Chicago test tracks, and signage
segments.summary: The Highway Trust Fund and a 90/10 federal-state funding split are described. The Chicago test tracks, where an Army company tested road materials, are covered, along with green reverse-message signage in Highway Gothic font.

segments.title: Highway revolts, construction, and design standards
segments.summary: Some wealthy communities revolted against routes through their neighborhoods. Jane Jacobs halted a Manhattan expressway through Soho and nearby areas, while poorer neighborhoods were often affected. The hosts describe design standards and the 55 mph speed limit, with Montana's speed law as a tangent.

segments.title: Listener mail on punk episode
segments.summary: A listener named Evan writes about the hardcore punk scene and his basement shows. The hosts close the mail segment and invite listener contact.
